Financial planning · Final loan payments · Visual planning guide

A balloon loan has two commitments: the regular payment and the final funding date

Compare regular payments with a fully amortizing loan, keep the remaining balloon visible, and calculate the separate saving needed to fund its due date.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Put the final balloon beside regular payments and a funding plan

Interactive planning lab

Regular monthly payment with the balloon$417.53
Monthly fund saving required under the selected return$156.99
Funding shortfall at the balloon date$2,844.03

One invented fixed-rate loan with monthly interest before each equal month-end payment. A selected principal amount remains as a separate balloon immediately after the final regular payment. The no-balloon comparison amortizes the same principal over the same months at the same rate. The fund is separate cash: its monthly return is converted from the entered effective annual net rate; each deposit arrives before the final balloon is due. No fees, missed payments, refinance approval, asset sale, collateral value or guaranteed fund return is assumed. The debt chart ends before payment of the balloon.

The central idea

A lower regular payment can leave principal for a later lump sum. A complete cash plan names that final obligation and the resources that will fund it, without assuming refinancing or a sale will be available.

01

Identify the principal that the regular payment leaves behind

A loan can use smaller regular payments while leaving a large principal amount for the end of the term. The regular payment and the final lump sum are both commitments. Looking only at the recurring debit can conceal the later funding need.

BDC’s glossary describes the balloon-payment concept in a business-lending context. The charts here use an original generic fixed-rate loan. They do not apply a BDC offer, a consumer-lending rule or an actual lender’s qualification criteria.

The default loan starts at CAD 25,000 with a 7% nominal annual rate and forty-eight month-end regular payments. Forty percent of the opening principal, or CAD 10,000, remains for a separate balloon immediately after the final regular payment. The comparison loan repays the same opening amount over the same forty-eight months without a balloon.

02

Compare the recurring payments and keep the interest convention explicit

Monthly interest is the opening balance multiplied by the 7% nominal annual rate divided by twelve. The fully amortizing loan requires approximately CAD 598.66 per month. The balloon version requires approximately CAD 417.53 per month, followed by the separate CAD 10,000 payment.

Both schedules use unrounded internal amounts. The balloon payment is included in the original payment calculation, so it is not an unexpected residual caused by rounding. An actual agreement may have different accrual, payment rounding, fees or a different definition of the final payment.

The lower regular payment leaves more debt outstanding for longer under these assumptions. The balloon schedule incurs about CAD 5,041.30 of interest across the term, compared with about CAD 3,735.49 for the fully amortizing schedule. Principal must still be repaid in both; the smaller recurring payment is not a reduction in the original amount borrowed.

03

Read the last month as a different cash date

The debt line ends after each regular payment and before payment of the balloon. It deliberately finishes at CAD 10,000 for the balloon choice. That point is an unpaid liability, rather than debt forgiveness or the balance after every obligation has been met.

The payment bars make the final month explicit. Its balloon-loan commitment is approximately CAD 417.53 + CAD 10,000 = CAD 10,417.53. The fully amortizing example has only its normal final regular payment under the unrounded convention.

Saving toward the balloon does not reduce that bill before the lender receives payment. A separate fund can supply the cash when needed, but it remains a separate household asset in the meantime. Counting a monthly fund transfer as both a loan principal repayment and retained savings would count the same money twice.

04

Put the selected saving amount beside the amount required

The example allocates CAD 2,000 to a balloon fund at the start and adds CAD 100 at each month-end. The fund earns a hypothetical 2% effective annual return after tax and costs, converted to an equivalent monthly compound rate.

Under those assumptions, the fund reaches about CAD 7,155.97 before the balloon payment. The remaining funding need is approximately CAD 2,844.03. The tool does not fill that gap with a new loan, presumed asset sale or an automatic account overdraft.

It separately solves the constant monthly saving that would reach CAD 10,000, given the selected opening cash, term and fund return. The default required amount is CAD 156.99 after rounding up to the nearest cent. Applying that rounded contribution throughout can leave a small surplus, which remains cash after the balloon is paid.

05

Test the saving plan without treating the fund return as guaranteed

The matrix varies month-end fund saving and the fund’s effective annual net return. Every cell retains the same loan, balloon amount, initial allocated cash and due date. A zero gap means that particular arithmetic schedule reaches the target.

At a zero fund return, the selected CAD 2,000 plus forty-eight CAD 100 deposits produces CAD 6,800, leaving CAD 3,200 unfunded. The contribution required at zero return is CAD 166.67 per month after rounding up. This isolates what the saving transfers can accomplish without growth.

A positive return reduces the modeled contribution requirement, but it is an assumption rather than an available offer. Money needed on a fixed date also needs appropriate access and risk terms. The calculator does not establish that an uncertain investment’s expected return can safely support the final loan obligation.

06

Check the combined budget without confusing transfers with costs

The recurring household commitment includes the regular loan payment and whatever cash is actually transferred to the balloon fund. With the selected CAD 100 saving, those transfers total about CAD 517.53 per month. Replacing it with the calculated required saving raises that total to about CAD 574.52 under the default assumptions.

Those monthly totals do not establish a complete wealth advantage over the fully amortizing loan. The balloon fund also starts with CAD 2,000 already allocated, and the two choices can leave different cash available elsewhere. A fair whole-household comparison must state what happens to that initial money and any differences in later monthly resources.

Verify an actual contract’s final amount, due date, charges and repayment conditions, then identify supported funding sources and their availability. Refinancing and selling an asset require their own evidence; they are not automatic outcomes of reaching maturity. The four charts keep the regular payment, unpaid principal and dated funding plan visible together.
